title: Temperature-tunable spin-wave refraction using superconducting control elements
authors: Pim H. Vree, Merel A. Bouma, Michael Borst, Tomas T. Osterholt, Rembert A. Duine, Toeno van der Sar
abstract: Spin waves are promising signal carriers for microwave control at the micrometer scale. However, realizing low-damping, tunable control of spin-wave propagation remains a central challenge. Here we use magnetic shielding by superconducting control elements to tune the local spin-wave dispersion and realize temperature-controlled refraction of spin waves in a thin-film magnetic insulator. Using magnetic imaging based on spins in diamond, we characterize the refractive index and demonstrate both positive and negative refraction as well as wavefront shaping by the superconductors. The observed refraction is explained by a geometrical analysis of the superconductivity-induced modification of the hyperbolic spin-wave dispersion. Our results demonstrate that superconductors enable tunable spin-wave optical elements, opening new opportunities for microwave control in classical or quantum information devices.
summary: The research reports on the use of superconducting elements to actively control spin-wave propagation within a YIG thin film. By tuning the local magnetic environment via superconductivity, the authors achieved temperature-tunable refraction and even negative refraction for spin waves. This opens pathways for developing novel microwave optical components for quantum or classical information processing.
main_problem: The central challenge addressed is achieving low-damping, tunable control of spin-wave propagation, specifically realizing temperature-controlled refraction.
main_result: The study successfully demonstrated temperature-tunable spin-wave refraction and the observation of negative refraction using superconducting elements integrated into a thin-film magnetic insulator structure.
method: Measurements involve exciting spin waves in YIG films and imaging their propagation characteristics (refraction, phase front shaping) using Nitrogen-Vacancy (NV) centers in diamond micromembranes as a sensitive detector.
model_or_system: The physical system is a thin-film magnetic insulator (YIG) coupled with superconducting control elements (NbTiN). The theoretical analysis models the superconductor's diamagnetic screening effect, which modifies the spin-wave dispersion relation based on the temperature-dependent London penetration depth.
key_observables: Spin wave refractive index, refraction angle ($	heta_{	ext{YIG/SC}}$), and the superconducting London penetration depth ($\lambda_L$).
important_parameters: Temperature ($T$), magnetic field components ($\mathbf{B}_{	ext{ip}}$), excitation frequency ($f_{	ext{ESR}}$), and interface angles.
main_assumptions: The small refraction observed above the superconducting critical temperature ($T_c$) is attributed to strain or damage-related anisotropy induced by deposition, rather than solely the superconducting effect.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate schematic setups (YIG/SC/NV), temperature dependence of refraction angles vs. setpoint temperature, and spatial maps showing phase front shaping and negative refraction regimes.
paper_structure: The paper systematically presents experimental measurements across various interface angles and temperatures, first demonstrating basic refraction, then quantifying the superconducting influence on dispersion ($\lambda_L$), and finally showcasing advanced control like negative refraction and beam translation.
why_interesting: This work demonstrates using superconductivity to engineer wave properties (refraction/dispersion) in classical magnetic systems, which has parallels with controlling photonic or magnonic modes in quantum devices.
